## Passages
RESULT [selftrain]: Few-shot fine-tuning with as few as 25 labelled target examples beat unsupervised domain-adaptive object detection in cross-crop comparisons. The authors conclude that choosing the source domain plus a little target supervision is more productive than a more sophisticated adaptation algorithm.
US [selftrain]: This argues for putting the human-labelling budget into a small, verified set from the robot's own field and camera, rather than relying on unlabelled harvested data plus clever adaptation. It also argues for the agent choosing which harvested sources are close to the target domain (DINOv2 or BioCLIP distance) before merging them.
CORRECTION [selftrain]: Submitted 2026-08-21, same authors. The abstract says 'few-shot fine-tuning with as few as 25 labeled target examples outperforms unsupervised DAOD'. The new cotton imagery is from UAVs.
RESULT [weeds]: Cotton->Soybean zero-shot: 57.8 mAP50. Soybean->Cotton zero-shot: 7.5 mAP50. Unsupervised DAOD lowered the score (distillation 50.3, adversarial 42.8). Fine-tuning with K=5/10/25 target labels gave 66.7/70.8/80.0 mAP50, and the full target set gave 84.9 against 76.8 for in-domain training alone. Conclusion: source selection plus modest target supervision beats algorithmic adaptation.
US [weeds]: Directly relevant to the incremental loop. A small, verified labelled increment from the target field (for example about 25 images reviewed by the labeller agent or a human) is worth more than a large unlabelled or pseudo-labelled harvest. Transfer is asymmetric, so which harvested source goes into the base matters and should be measured per source. That is the same attribution question the rollba [note truncated at collection]
CORRECTION [weeds]: All numbers match for Cotton->Soybean (57.8 zero-shot; distillation 50.3, adversarial 42.8; K=5/10/25 give 66.7/70.8/80.0; full target 84.9 vs in-domain 76.8), and Soybean->Cotton zero-shot 7.5 is correct.
